rv.q: Truth be told, I found the play "Sisters" at Writers Theatre to be something of a miserable experience.
In telling a life story with such minimal tools — a human body, a human voice — “Sisters” feels like it isn’t just about humanity, it’s humanity itself.
SISTERS is a moving and powerful theatrical experience.
Libby's Sisters is a refreshing, insightful look at our relationship with these technological marvels we created.

But though the language in Libby’s play is often adroit, pointed, and poetic, to me at least the script feels like a very good short sci-fi story being enacted by talented actors, rather than a play with a true dramatic arc.
While the play's premise and subsequent subject matter are thought-provoking, it is difficult to feel a strong emotional connection to the characters in this one-woman (plus her AI companion) show.
But in 2026, the play feels obsolete.
But one excellent performance is not nearly enough, and 95 minutes is far too long for a concept this thin.

On the tech side, the costumes ( Lia Wallfish), lighting (Eric Watkins) and co-projection design by Stephan Mazurek & Liz Sung allow us to see, and feel the time go by, setting us up for a dynamite and very special ending.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this AI-themed drama about a woman and her computer sister over 90 years. While some praise its intellectual ambition and performances, others find it emotionally distant and unable to meaningfully explore its timely premise.
